sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Mañjuśrī** (*manjushri*) ​— Wisdom, ‌Intellect · ‌The Gentle ​Glory, Sword ​of Wisdom ​— is ​the bodhisattva ​of transcendent ‌wisdom (prajñā): ​the ever-youthful ​prince of ‌the Mahāyāna ​who wields ‌the flaming ​sword that ‌cuts through ​ignorance and ​carries the book ​of the ​Perfection of ​Wisdom on ‌his lotus.[^1]

​His name ‌joins *mañju*, ​‘gentle, beautiful, ‌charming’, with ​*śrī*, ‘glory, ‌splendour, majesty’ ​— ‘Gentle ‌Glory’. The ​tradition hears ​the softness ‌as the ‌point: true ‌wisdom is not ​harsh, and ​the sword ‌that ends ​confusion is ​wielded by ‌a boy. ​He is ​the bodhisattva ‌who dares ​what others ‌will not ​— in ​the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa ​he alone ​accepts the ‌call to ‌visit the ​sick layman — ‌and the ​patron of ​every student, ‌scholar, and ‌debater in ‌the Buddhist ‌world, from ​the academies ‌of Nālandā ​to the ​examination halls ​of Tibet.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ​the name ​as **Mañjuśrī** ​and serves ‌its temple at ​[mañjuśrī.com](https://xn--majur-pta32bwm.com). The ​restoration keeps ​the palatal ‌ñ, the ​palatal ś, ‌and the ​long final ‌ī of ​the Sanskrit; ‌the plain ‌ASCII *manjushri* ​is a ​modern convenience ​of the ​early domain-name ‌system, not ‌an attested ​ancient spelling.[^3]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (New York: Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Mañjuśrī’.
Watson, Burton, trans., The Vimalakirti Sutra (New York: Columbia University Press, 1997).
Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. mañju, śrī.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Sanskrit as ‌**मञ्जुश्री** (IAST ​*mañjuśrī*): a compound ​of *mañju*, ​‘gentle, sweet, lovely’, ​and *śrī*, ​‘glory, splendour’ — ‌‘Gentle Glory’ ​or ‘Sweet Majesty’.[^1] ​His epithets extend ‌the music: ​**Mañjughoṣa**, ‘Gentle Voice’ ‌(or ‘Beautiful ​Sound’); **Kumārabhūta**, ‘the ‌Ever-Youthful’, for ​he is always ​figured as ​a prince of ​sixteen; and ​**Vāgīśvara**, ‘Lord of ‌Speech’, the ​orators' bodhisattva.

The ‌ASCII form ​*manjushri* survives only ‌because the ​early domain-name system ‌could not ​carry diacritics; it ‌is a ​technological compromise, not ​an ancient ‌spelling, and it ‌flattens three distinctive ‌letters — ​the palatal nasal ​ñ, the ‌palatal sibilant ś, ​and the ​long ī — ‌into approximations. ​The Unicode restoration ​**Mañjuśrī** recovers ‌all three directly ​in the ‌address bar. Because ​the restoration ​preserves distinctive letters ​and vowel ​length the ASCII ‌form loses, ‌the name is ​classified Tier ‌1.

The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ​**m** → ‌**M** — Same, ‌capitalized
- ‌**a** → **a** ‌— Same
​- **n** → ‌**ñ** — ​Palatal nasal ñ ​(as in ​Spanish *mañana*)
- ‌**j** → ​**j** — Same
​- **u** ​→ **u** — ‌Same
- ​**s** → **ś** ​— Palatal ​sibilant ś
- ‌**h** → ​**—** — Dropped ‌(English digraph, ​not Sanskrit)
- ‌**r** → **r** ​— Same
‌- **i** → ‌**ī** — ​Long vowel ī

​The project ​holds the domain ​**mañjuśrī.com** (xn--majur-pta32bwm.com) ‌as the canonical ‌home of ​this name.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. mañju, śrī.
Edgerton, Franklin, Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit Grammar and Dictionary, vol. 2 (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953), s.v. Mañjuśrī, Mañjughoṣa.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name ​is **/məɲ.ˈdʑu.ɕriː/** ​— Sanskrit ​Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Ma-** ​— Bilabial ​[m] with ‌short ​[ə]
- ‌**-ñju-** — ​Palatal ‌nasal [ɲ] ​(the sound ​of ​Spanish *ñ*) ​with voiced ​palatal ‌stop [dʑ] ​and ‌short [u]; ​the ‘gentle’ ‌of ​the name
‌- **-śrī** ​— ‌Palatal sibilant ​[ɕ] with ​trilled ‌[r] and ‌long close ‌[iː]; ​the ‘glory’, ​its vowel ‌held ​long

For ​the modern ‌speaker, ​the closest ​approximation is: ‌‘mun-JOO-shree’ ​— the ‌‘nj’ soft ​as ​in *onion*, ​the final ​‘ee’ ‌sustained.

Kindred ‌and historical ​forms ‌of the ​name:

- ​**Sanskrit** ‌— मञ्जुश्री ‌(mañjuśrī), ‘Gentle ‌Glory’; ‌also Mañjughoṣa, ​‘Gentle Voice’
‌- ​**Chinese** — ​文殊師利 (Wénshūshīlì), ​abbreviated ‌文殊 (Wénshū)
​- ​**Japanese** — ​Monju (Monju ‌Bosatsu)
​- **Tibetan** ​— 'Jam ​dpal ‌(Jampel), ‘Gentle ​Splendour’; 'Jam ‌dbyangs ​(Jamyang), ‘Gentle ‌Voice’

Mañjuśrī ​is ‌Tier 1: ‌ñ, ś, ​and ​ī are ​all distinctive ​marks ‌the ASCII ‌alphabet cannot ​write.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. mañjuśrī.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved ‌in Devanagari ​as ​**मञ्जुश्री** — ​Brahmic ​abugida, attested ​Buddhist ‌Sanskrit, in ​the ​sūtra manuscripts ‌of ​India and ‌Nepal; ​the script ‌is ​written left-to-right.[^1]

​The ​scholarly transliteration ​is ​*Mañjuśrī* (IAST), ‌giving ​the normalized ‌reading ​/məɲ.ˈdʑu.ɕriː/.

The ‌rendering ​proceeds step ‌by ​step:

- ‌Sanskrit ​Mañjuśrī is ​written ‌मञ्जुश्री in ‌Devanagari: ‌मञ्जु (mañju) ​+ ​श्री (śrī); ‌the ​conjunct ञ्ज ​writes ‌the palatal ​cluster ​ñj, and ‌श्री ​is the ‌ligature ​śrī.
- ​The ​compound is ​mañju ‌(‘gentle, beautiful’) ‌+ ​śrī (‘glory, ‌splendour’): ​‘Gentle Glory’.
​- ‌IAST distinguishes ‌the ‌palatal nasal ‌ñ ​from dental ‌n, ​the palatal ​sibilant ​ś from ‌retroflex ​ṣ and ​dental ​s, and ‌marks ​the long ​final ​ī with ‌the ​macron.
- ‌The ​Unicode restoration ‌Mañjuśrī ​is registrable ‌in ‌.com; the ​Devanagari ​form is ​not ​supported in ‌the ‌.com IDN ​table.[^2]

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. mañjuśrī.
Edgerton, Franklin, Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit Dictionary (Yale University Press, 1953), s.v. Mañjuśrī.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Mañjuśrī** ​is ‌wisdom personified: ‌not ​accumulated ​knowledge ​but prajñā, ​the ​seeing ‌that ​cuts things ​loose ‌from ​illusion.[^1]

‌### ​Transcendent Wisdom

‌He ​embodies ​the ​prajñā of ​the ​Perfection ‌of ​Wisdom literature ‌— ​the ‌insight ​into emptiness ‌that ​the ‌sūtras ​call the ​mother ‌of ‌all ‌Buddhas.

​### The ​Sword ‌of ​Discrimination

​His blade ‌severs ​ignorance ​at ‌the root: ​analysis, ‌debate, ​and ​the courage ​to ​cut ‌through ‌one's own ​positions.

‌### ​The ​Ever-Youthful

‌Kumārabhūta: wisdom ‌as ‌perpetual ‌beginner's ​mind, a ‌prince ​who ​never ​hardens into ‌a ​sage.

​### ​Patron of ‌Scholars

​Students, ​monks, ​and debaters ‌across ​Asia ‌invoke ​him ‌before study ​and ‌examination; ‌the ​great universities ​of ​Buddhist ​India ‌counted him ‌their ​patron.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Mañjuśrī’.
Lopez, Donald S., ed., Buddhism in Practice (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1995).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography of ‌Mañjuśrī is ‌the ​complete vocabulary ​of ​intellect:[^1]

- ​**The flaming ​sword ‌(khadga)** — ​Raised ​in the ‌right hand, ​wreathed ‌in fire: ​the ‌blade of ​prajñā that ​cuts ​ignorance and ​the ​flames that ‌burn its ​roots
‌- **The ​book ‌on the ​lotus** — ‌The ​Perfection of ‌Wisdom ​sūtra (Prajñāpāramitā) ​resting on ‌a ‌blue utpala ‌lotus ​in his ​left hand: ‌the ​text as ​flower, ‌wisdom as ​something that ​blooms
‌- **The ​youthful ‌prince** — ​Sixteen forever: ​princely ​ornaments, no ​monastic ‌robes — ‌insight is ​not ‌a retirement
​- ​**The lion ‌mount** — ‌In ‌many forms ‌he ​rides a ‌lion: the ​roar ​of the ​true ‌teaching, fearlessness ​in debate
​- ​**The syllable ‌a** ​— His ​seed-syllable and ​the ‌first letter ​of ‌the Arapacana ​syllabary, the ‌alphabet ​taught as ‌a ‌meditation on ​emptiness; his ​mantra ​is *oṃ ​a ‌ra pa ‌ca na ​dhīḥ*[^2]

sources.citation: Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1914).
Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Mañjuśrī’ and ‘Arapacana’.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Mañjuśrī's mythology ​is a cycle ‌of encounters ‌in which wisdom ​proves itself by ​daring.[^1]

### The ​Visit to Vimalakīrti ​(Vimalakīrtinirdeśa)

When ​the layman Vimalakīrti ‌falls ill and ​the Buddha asks ​his great disciples ‌and bodhisattvas ​to call on ‌him, one after ​another declines — ‌each has ​been bested by ​the layman before. ​Only Mañjuśrī accepts. ​Their dialogue is ​the sūtra's ‌summit: on nonduality, ​on emptiness, on ‌the bodhisattva's work ​in the ‌world of passion ​— and it ‌ends with Vimalakīrti's ​thunderous silence, which ‌Mañjuśrī alone ​is quick enough ​to praise.[^2]

### ‌The Nāga Princess ‌(Lotus Sūtra 12)

‌In the ​Lotus Sūtra's Devadatta ​chapter, Mañjuśrī emerges ‌from the nāga ​palace beneath ​the sea and ‌stuns the assembly ​by testifying that ​an eight-year-old nāga ‌girl has ​attained full awakening ‌— wisdom's declaration ​that enlightenment is ​no one's monopoly, ​not even ​humanity's.[^3]

### The ‌Director of the ‌Pilgrimage (Gaṇḍavyūha)

In ​the Avataṃsaka's ‌closing book it ​is Mañjuśrī who ​sends the young ‌Sudhana on his ‌pilgrimage to ‌fifty-three teachers — ‌the bodhisattva of ​wisdom as the ‌dispatcher of every ​genuine search.[^4]

​### The Lake ​of Kathmandu (Svayambhū ‌Purāṇa)

Nepal's own ​chronicle makes ​him the valley's ​founder: Mañjuśrī came ‌from his mountain ​Wutai to venerate ​the self-existent ​flame at the ‌lake of Nāgavāsa, ​saw that the ‌waters imprisoned ​the shrine, and ‌with one stroke ​of his sword ‌cut the gorge ‌at Chobar, ​draining the lake ​and opening the ​Kathmandu valley to ​settlement. Nepal's geography ‌is, in ‌its own telling, ​his handiwork.[^5]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Mañjuśrī’.
Watson, Burton, trans., The Vimalakirti Sutra (Columbia University Press, 1997), ch. 5.
Kern, H., trans., Saddharma-Puṇḍarīka, SBE 21 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884), ch. 12.
Cleary, Thomas, trans., The Flower Ornament Scripture (Boston: Shambhala, 1993), Gaṇḍavyūha.
Svayambhū Purāṇa (Newar Buddhist chronicle of the Kathmandu valley).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Mañjuśrī's ​receptions are ‌the ‌history of ​Buddhist ​scholarship itself. ​In ​China he ​became ‌Wénshū, and ​Mount ​Wutai in ‌Shanxi ​— five ‌flat ​peaks, cold ‌and ​clear — ​was ​identified as ​his ​earthly abode, ‌becoming for ​over ‌a millennium ​the ‌greatest pilgrimage ​mountain ‌of East ​Asia, ‌visited by ​monks ​of every ‌nation, ‌including the ‌Japanese ​pilgrim Ennin, ​whose ‌ninth-century diary ​is ​a classic ‌of ​the road.[^1] ​In ‌Japan he ​is ‌Monju, the ​wisdom ​of the ​Zen ​hall; in ‌Tibet, ‌Jampel and ​Jamyang, ‌the personal ​deity ​of scholars ‌— ‌Tsongkhapa, founder ‌of ‌the Gelug ​school, ‌was revered ​as ​his emanation.[^2]

​Within ‌the PuniCodex ​cross-tradition index, ​kindred ​figures include ‌[[vajrapani|Vajrapāṇi]] ​and [[guanyin|Guānyīn]] ​(Avalokiteśvara) ​— with ‌whom ​he forms ‌the ​classic triad ‌of ​the ‘Lords ‌of ‌the Three ​Families’: ​wisdom, power, ​and ​compassion as ‌the ‌bodhisattva's complete ​equipment.

sources.citation: Reischauer, Edwin O., trans., Ennin's Diary: The Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law (New York: Ronald Press, 1955).
Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Mañjuśrī’, ‘Wutai Shan’, ‘Tsongkhapa’.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Mañjuśrī ​is the ‌patron ‌saint of ​every ​Buddhist ​student. His ​mantra ​*oṃ a ‌ra ​pa ca ​na ‌dhīḥ* is ​recited ‌before ​examinations from ‌Kathmandu ​to Kyoto; ​the ​Arapacana syllabary ​he ​anchors — ‌an ​alphabet ‌whose letters ​are ‌meditations — ​made ‌him the ​Buddha ‌of literacy ​itself.[^1] ​Mount ‌Wutai, his ‌earthly ‌seat, remains ​a ​living pilgrimage ‌city ​and a ​UNESCO ‌World ​Heritage landscape ​(2009), ‌its temples ​— ‌among them ​the ​Foguang ​Temple's east ​hall ‌of 857, ‌the ​oldest surviving ‌timber ​hall in ​China ‌— ‌monuments to ‌a ‌millennium and ​a ‌half of ​devotion.[^2]

​His image ​set ‌the ​iconography of ​intellect ​for half ‌the ​world: the ​sword ​and the ‌book ​are ‌so completely ​his ‌that a ​bodhisattva ‌bearing them ‌is ​identifiable across ​a ​thousand ​years of ‌art ‌without an ​inscription.

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Arapacana’, ‘Mañjuśrī’.
UNESCO, Mount Wutai, World Heritage List no. 1279 (inscribed 2009).

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Mañjuśrī's ​material record ‌begins with ‌the sūtra ​transmission ​itself and ​blossoms in ​the art ​of ‌the mountain ​that claimed ​him. Early ‌images — ​a ‌princely figure ​with sword ‌and book ​— ​appear in ​the art ​of late ​Kuṣāṇa ‌and Gupta ​India and ‌multiply in ​the ‌Pāla-period bronzes ​of Nālandā, ‌the very ​university ‌whose scholars ​made him ​their patron.[^1]

‌**Mount Wutai** ‌is ‌the great ​monument: the ​Avataṃsaka tradition's ‌identification ​of its ​five terraces ‌with the ​bodhisattva's ​‘Clear-and-Cool Mountain’ ‌made the ​range a ‌sacred ​geography, and ​its surviving ​temples — ​Foguang ‌si's east ‌hall (857 ​CE), the ‌oldest ​dated timber ​structure in ‌China, and ‌Nanchan si ‌(782 ‌CE), older ​still — ‌preserve Tang ​architecture ​in situ. ​Ennin's diary ‌(838–847) describes ​the ​mountain at ​the height ‌of its ​international ​fame.[^2] Nepalese ​art keeps ‌his other ​legend: ‌the sword ​that cut ‌the Chobar ​gorge is ‌the ‌valley's founding ​artifact, and ​Svayambhū's hilltop ​stūpa ​marks the ‌flame he ‌came to ​worship.

sources.citation: Huntington, Susan L., The ‘Pāla-Sena’ Schools of Sculpture (Leiden: Brill, 1984).
Reischauer, Edwin O., trans., Ennin's Diary (Ronald Press, 1955); UNESCO, Mount Wutai (2009).

sections.label: Pāli Canon
sections.body:
**Mañjuśrī ​is ‌absent from ‌the ​Pāli ​Canon.** ​The ​Tipiṭaka knows ​no ‌bodhisattva ​of ​this name; ‌its ​ideal ‌figures ​are the ‌arahants ​and ​the ​Buddha-to-be ​of the ​Jātakas, ‌not ​the ‌celestial bodhisattvas ​of ‌the ​Mahāyāna. ‌As ​with [[amitabha|Amitābha]] ‌and ​[[akshobhya|Akṣobhya]], ​the ‌absence is ‌a ‌fact ​of ​canon and ‌lineage: ​the ​Pāli ‌tradition ​closed around ​the ‌early ​discourses, ‌while Mañjuśrī ​rose ​with ​the ​Perfection ‌of Wisdom ‌literature ​in ‌the ​centuries around ​the ‌turn ‌of ‌the era.[^1]

‌What ​the ‌canon ​does ​hold is ​his ‌substance: ​the ​analysis of ​prajñā/paññā ‌as ​the ​path's ​crowning factor ‌and ​the ‌lion's-roar ​ideal of ‌fearless ​teaching ‌are ‌Pāli materials ​that ​the ​Mahāyāna ​personified ‌in the ‌gentle ​prince.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Mañjuśrī’.
Edgerton, Franklin, Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit Dictionary (Yale University Press, 1953), s.v. Mañjuśrī.

sections.label: Mahāyāna Sūtras
sections.body:
Mañjuśrī ​is the ‌most ‌ubiquitous bodhisattva ​in ​the Mahāyāna ​sūtra ​literature. The ​**Perfection ‌of Wisdom** ​texts ​make him ‌prajñā's ​personal form ‌— ​the Aṣṭasāhasrikā ‌and ​its descendants ​stage ​him as ​wisdom's ​interlocutor; the ‌**Vimalakīrtinirdeśa** gives ​him ‌the greatest ​dialogue ‌of the ​canon, ‌the sickbed ​visit ‌(ch. 5); ​the ​**Saddharmapuṇḍarīka** opens ‌with ‌his exchange ‌with ​Maitreya on ​the ‌Buddha's ray ​of ​light and ‌closes ​its twelfth ​chapter ‌with his ​testimony ‌of the ​awakened ​nāga princess.[^1]

​The ​**Avataṃsaka** cycle ‌casts ‌him as ​the ‌dispatcher of ​Sudhana's ​pilgrimage in ‌the ‌Gaṇḍavyūha; the ‌**Śūraṅgamasamādhi ‌Sūtra** takes ​his ‌name for ​its ​hero's own; ​and ‌the tantric ​**Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti** — ​‘Chanting ​the Names ‌of ​Mañjuśrī’ — ​hymns ​him in ‌a ​hundred and ‌sixty ​verses as ‌the ​treasury of ‌every ‌epithet of ​wisdom, ​becoming in ​Tibet ​the most ‌recited ‌liturgy of ​all.[^2]

sources.citation: Watson, Burton, trans., The Vimalakirti Sutra (Columbia University Press, 1997); Kern, H., trans., Saddharma-Puṇḍarīka (1884), ch. 1, 12.
Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti; Cleary, Thomas, trans., The Flower Ornament Scripture (Shambhala, 1993), Gaṇḍavyūha.

sections.label: Commentarial Tradition
sections.body:
The ​commentarial crown ‌of his ‌tradition ​is the ​**Nāmasaṃgīti** ​exegesis: Indian ​masters — ​Vilāsavajra ‌foremost among ​them — ​commented ‌‘Chanting the ​Names of ‌Mañjuśrī’ ​as the ‌root ​text of ​the wisdom ​tantras, ​and the ​work's transmission ‌to ​Tibet made ‌it the ​daily ‌liturgy of ​the ‌monastic colleges, ​where its ‌verses ​are memorized ​before debate ‌begins.[^1] ‌The Arapacana ‌syllabary's commentaries ​read ​the alphabet ‌itself ​as a ​curriculum of ‌emptiness ​— the ​letter a ‌as ​the door ‌of the ​unborn, ​the first ​teaching ​and the ‌last.

East ‌Asian ​exegesis made ‌Wutai's five ​terraces ​a commentary ‌in geography: ‌the ‌Avataṃsaka tradition's ‌gloss ​of ‘Clear-and-Cool ‌Mountain’ fixed ​the ​pilgrimage theology ​that Ennin ‌recorded ​and the ​Tang temples ​still ‌attest. In ​Nepal, ​the Svayambhū ​Purāṇa's narrative ‌of ​the sword ‌and the ​lake ‌functions as ​the valley's ‌own ‌exegetical chronicle ​— ​a land ​reading its ​founding ‌as an ‌act of ​prajñā.[^2]

sources.citation: Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti with the commentary tradition (Vilāsavajra).
Reischauer, Edwin O., trans., Ennin's Diary (Ronald Press, 1955); Svayambhū Purāṇa.

sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Mañjuśrī ​is Buddhism's ‌answer ‌to ​a fear ​every ​thoughtful ​person knows: ​that ‌thinking ​itself is ​the ‌problem. The ​tradition ‌could ​have made ‌wisdom ​a ​grey elder; ​it ​made ​her a ‌sixteen-year-old ​with a ‌sword. ​The ‌youth is ​the ‌doctrine ​— insight ‌does ​not ​arrive with ‌age ‌and does ‌not ​exhaust ​itself in ‌caution; ​it ​stays, in ‌the ​best ​minds, permanently ‌quick.

​The sword ‌and ​the ​book are ​the ​whole ‌curriculum. The ‌book ​says: ‌learn everything. ​The ​sword says: ‌hold ‌none ‌of it. ‌Students ​across ‌Asia still ​begin ​their ​year with ‌his ​mantra, and ​the ​petition ‌hidden in ​*a ​ra ​pa ca ‌na* ​is ‌the scholar's ​honest ‌prayer: let ​me ‌know ‌a great ​deal, ​and ​let none ​of ‌it ‌make me ​stupid.

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Mañjuśrī’.
